notes: Cost spectrum: 0.1 = barely matters (regional/allophonic variation), 0.3 = noticeable but understandable, 0.5 = significant error (mispronunciation), 0.8 = very wrong (changes meaning or comprehension), 1.0 = max default substitution cost.
english_speaker_error: true means this is a typical pattern produced by an L1 English speaker speaking Spanish. The UI surfaces these in feedback ('your ñ came out as n').

Pairs are directional: 'expected' is the target Spanish phoneme, 'actual' is what the model detected. The matrix applies regardless of order in scoring (symmetric lookup), but description is written from the L1-English direction for clarity.

matrix.description: ñ pronounced as plain n (mañana → manana, canyon → cannon). Comprehensible but obviously non-native.
ñ produced as a literal n+y sequence rather than a single palatal nasal. Very close; native listeners barely notice.
Trilled rr softened to a single tap (perro → pero — meaning shift from 'dog' to 'but', but listeners usually disambiguate by context).
Trilled rr replaced with English alveolar approximant. Heavy English-accent marker.
Spanish tap replaced with English alveolar approximant; the most pervasive English-accent tell.
Single tap over-trilled. Sounds emphatic but understandable.
Tap rendered as English /d/ (Spanish ɾ and American flapped 'tt' in 'butter' are nearly identical, so this is often correct in disguise; cost stays low).
Voiceless velar fricative simplified to plain English /h/. Latin American /x/ is already close to /h/; minimal penalty.
Voiceless velar fricative replaced with stop (jamón → kamón). Significant error; changes phonemic identity.
Spanish j read as English j sound (jamás → jamas with English 'j'). Breaks comprehension.
ll merged to /j/ — yeísmo. Default Latin American pronunciation; not an error.
ll as palatal fricative — yeísmo variant. Not an error.
ll flattened to plain l (calle → cale). Comprehension-impacting.
ll as /ʃ/ — Argentine/Uruguayan sheísmo. Regional variant, not an error.
Palatal fricative softened to approximant — common allophonic variation.
y produced as English j (yo → joh). Heavy English-accent marker.
Spanish v read as English /v/ labiodental rather than /b/ bilabial (vino → English-vino instead of bee-noh).
Intervocalic b/v read as English /v/ instead of bilabial approximant.
Approximant produced as full stop. Allophonic; native speakers do this in emphatic speech.
Stop softened to approximant. Allophonic.
Intervocalic d produced as full stop instead of approximant. Allophonic; emphatic-register.
Stop softened to approximant in casual register.
Voiced dental approximant devoiced to English 'th' as in 'think' (nada → English-nath-uh). Comprehension-impacting.
Approximant produced as full stop. Allophonic.
Soft English /g/ used before e/i (gente → English-jen-tay). Spanish g before e/i is /x/, not /dʒ/ — heavy error, breaks comprehension.
Stop softened to approximant. Allophonic.
Spanish /a/ reduced to schwa in unstressed syllables (English habit). Spanish vowels do not reduce; this is a major accent marker.
Spanish /e/ reduced to schwa in unstressed syllables.
Spanish /o/ reduced to schwa in unstressed syllables (libros → English-lee-brəs).
Spanish /e/ produced as English short-i. Common when speaker tries to avoid the 'eh' lengthening.
Spanish /e/ diphthongized to English 'ay' (de → 'day' instead of 'deh').
Spanish /o/ diphthongized to English 'oh-w' (no → 'know' instead of 'noh').
Spanish /i/ produced as English short-i (sí → 'sih' instead of 'see').
Spanish /u/ produced as English short-u (tú → 'tuh' instead of 'too').
Spanish /u/ glided to English /ju/ (Cuba → 'kyu-bah' instead of 'KOO-bah'). Common after stops.
Spanish unaspirated /p/ produced with English aspiration. Accent marker, not comprehension-impacting.
Spanish unaspirated /t/ produced with English aspiration.
Spanish unaspirated /k/ produced with English aspiration.
English-style flapping of /t/ between vowels (Spanish /t/ stays a clean dental stop).
Spanish /s/ voiced to /z/ (casa → 'kaza'). Spanish lacks phonemic /z/ — error.
Castilian distinción: c/z → /θ/, s → /s/. Regional variant, not Latin American but understood.
Spanish 'ch' weakened to English 'sh' (mucho → musho). Northern Mexican variant exists but for L1 English it's an error.
Speaker pronounces a silent Spanish h (hola → 'hoh-lah' with audible h instead of 'OH-lah'). Insertion.
Speaker inserts an epenthetic schwa between consonants in clusters (ps-, ts-) where Spanish does not.
Final s dropped (buenas tardes → buena tarde). Common in some Caribbean dialects (not error there) but typical L1-English error in Latin American target.
Tap r dropped entirely in clusters or codas. Comprehension-impacting.
Final n dropped (hablan → habla). Changes verb agreement.
Speaker breaks rising diphthong into two syllables (siete → 'see-eh-teh' instead of 'SYEH-teh'). Comprehensible but rhythm is off.
Speaker breaks rising diphthong (bueno → 'boo-eh-noh' instead of 'BWEH-noh').
Voicing error on /f/. Uncommon for L1 English but model-confusion plausible.
